concept_panel.title: Relational vs NoSQL Databases
concept_panel.explanation: Relational databases organize data into tables with schemas, keys, constraints, and joins. NoSQL systems trade some relational structure for document flexibility, in-memory speed, high write volume, or specialized access patterns. PostgreSQL is a strong default for relational workloads; MongoDB fits document-shaped data; Redis is usually a fast cache or ephemeral store. The interview skill is matching data shape and correctness needs to the storage model.
key_takeaways: Relational databases fit joins and constraints.
Document stores fit flexible nested records.
Redis is usually used for fast cache/session access.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can choose storage based on data shape and guarantees.
concept_panel.practical_example: Orders that reference users and need financial reports are usually a relational fit.

questions.prompt: Orders must reference users and support financial reports. Which database model fits first?

concept_panel.title: Keys, Relationships, and JOINs
concept_panel.explanation: Primary keys uniquely identify rows, and foreign keys connect rows across tables. JOINs combine related rows so normalized data can answer richer questions. Many-to-many relationships usually need a junction table. This is foundational because database schema design determines both correctness and query performance.
key_takeaways: Primary keys identify rows.
Foreign keys model relationships.
JOINs reconstruct related data at query time.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand relational modeling, not just SQL syntax.
concept_panel.practical_example: orders.user_id references users.id, letting a query join orders to the owning user.

questions.explanation: JOIN type controls which unmatched rows are kept while combining related tables.

concept_panel.title: Transactions and ACID
concept_panel.explanation: A transaction groups related database changes so they commit together or roll back together. ACID describes guarantees around atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. This matters when partial updates would corrupt business invariants, such as money transfers. Stronger transaction guarantees protect correctness but can reduce concurrency.
key_takeaways: Atomicity means all-or-nothing changes.
Isolation controls concurrent behavior.
Use transactions to protect invariants.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand data correctness under concurrent changes.
concept_panel.practical_example: Debit one account and credit another inside one transaction.

questions.prompt: Read traffic is high but writes fit on one primary database. What can help reads?
questions.explanation: Read replicas copy data for serving reads. They are not the same as sharding because all data is still replicated.

concept_panel.title: Replication and Replica Lag
concept_panel.explanation: Replication copies data from a primary or leader to follower replicas. It can improve read capacity and availability, but followers may lag behind recent writes. A user who writes to the leader and immediately reads from a lagging replica may see stale data. The design must decide which reads require freshness.
key_takeaways: Replicas help read scale and availability.
Replica lag creates stale-read risk.
Read-your-writes may require leader reads or session-aware routing.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand consistency trade-offs in replicated systems.
concept_panel.practical_example: After updating a profile, route that user's next profile read to the leader until replicas catch up.

questions.prompt: One database cannot hold the data volume or write load. Which approach splits data?
questions.explanation: Sharding partitions data across nodes. It increases scale but complicates routing and cross-shard queries.

concept_panel.title: Sharding and Hot Partitions
concept_panel.explanation: Sharding splits data across nodes so one machine does not hold all data or write load. The shard key decides where each record goes. A poor key can concentrate traffic on one shard and create a hot partition. Sharding increases capacity but makes routing, rebalancing, and cross-shard operations harder.
key_takeaways: Sharding partitions data across nodes.
Shard-key choice controls balance.
Skew creates hot shards and operational pain.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand horizontal scaling and data distribution failures.
concept_panel.practical_example: Partitioning by tenant_type can overload the enterprise shard if enterprise tenants dominate traffic.

questions.prompt: A social like count is briefly stale after a write. Which model can accept that?
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency accepts temporary staleness when immediate correctness is not required.

concept_panel.title: Consistency vs Availability
concept_panel.explanation: Consistency describes what reads are allowed to observe after writes. Some invariants, like unique usernames or bank balances, need strong consistency. Other values, like social counters, can often be eventually consistent. During failures, stronger consistency may reduce availability because coordination is required.
key_takeaways: Use strong consistency for hard invariants.
Eventual consistency can fit counters and feeds.
Consistency choices trade off with latency and availability.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can choose guarantees based on business invariants.
concept_panel.practical_example: A like count can lag briefly, but a payment ledger should not accept conflicting balances.

questions.prompt: A query scans millions of users for every login by email. What is likely missing?
questions.explanation: A lookup by email should usually use an index, otherwise the database may scan every row.

concept_panel.title: Database Indexes
concept_panel.explanation: An index is an extra data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning everything. Indexes are useful for frequent filters, joins, and ordering. They are not free: every write may need to update the index, and indexes consume storage. Good answers tie indexes to specific query patterns.
key_takeaways: Indexes speed reads for matching access paths.
Indexes add write and storage cost.
Index choice should follow real queries.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand SQL query performance trade-offs.
concept_panel.practical_example: A login query by email should usually have an index on users.email.
